You express concession (an obstacle that doesn’t stop the action): aunque + indicative / subjunctive, a pesar de (que), por mucho que, por más que, por muy… que, aun así, y eso que.
However much I study, the subjunctive won’t go into my head.
Even though I’m tired, I’m going to class.
Although he lives far away, he comes every Tuesday.
However hard it is, I won’t give up.
She speaks well, and that’s even though she’s only been learning for a year.
To review aunque + indicative (fact) / + subjunctive (hypothesis or a fact you don’t dispute).
To use por mucho que / por más que + subjunctive.
To use por muy + adjective + que + subjunctive.
To use a pesar de + infinitive / a pesar de que + verb.
To use y eso que and aun así in conversation.
September, a month before the wedding in Kyoto. After class, Costel, the lorry driver, stays behind in the classroom. He looks sad. Ana sits down next to him.
Miss, I think I’m going to quit the course. However much I study, I can’t manage to speak well.
What do you mean, quit? You’ve made huge progress, and that’s even though you drive twelve hours a day.
Even if I’ve made progress, it isn’t enough. My grandson doesn’t understand me.
Your grandson? I didn’t know you had a grandson in Spain.
Yes. My daughter has lived in Valencia for ten years. She married a man from Valencia. The boy is six and only speaks Spanish. Well, and Valencian.
And doesn’t your daughter speak Romanian to him?
Although she tried, the boy didn’t want to. He says Romanian is “weird”. When I go to see him, he smiles at me, but we can’t talk. However affectionate he is, he gets bored with me.
Costel, listen to me. However hard it is for you, you can’t give up now. You’re doing it for him.
I know. But I’m fifty-eight. At my age, my head isn’t what it used to be.
Mrs Ecaterina is eighty and she went to Colombia. And Mr Dan learned to tell his son he’s proud of him. Even so, do you think you’re too old?
(smiles a little) Put like that… But what can I do? However much I repeat the conjugations, when I’m with the boy my mind goes blank.
Then don’t talk to him about conjugations. What does the boy like?
Lorries. He’s crazy about lorries. He has a huge collection.
Well, there you go! Even if you don’t know much Spanish, you know more about lorries than anyone. Let’s prepare a conversation about lorries. And next time, he’ll be the one left open-mouthed.
“y eso que” = and that’s even though
“aunque haya mejorado” = even if I’ve made progress (subj.)
“quedarse en blanco” = for your mind to go blank
por-MOO-cho-keh: stress on MOO. Said emphatically, it shows effort: «¡Por MUcho que estudie…!»
ee-EH-so-keh: run together. Used in conversation for a surprise: «Habla bien, y eso que…»
keh-DAR-seh-en-BLAN-ko: “to go blank”, when you forget everything because of nerves.
1. Aunque: review and a new shade
a hypothesis OR a known fact you don’t dispute
Aunque está cansado, viene. (I know he’s tired.)
Aunque esté cansado, vendrá. (He may be, it doesn’t matter.)
Aunque ha mejorado, no habla bien.
Aunque haya mejorado, no es suficiente. (I accept he’s improved, but…)

The new B1 shade: the subjunctive with “aunque” can also show a REAL fact that the speaker acknowledges but considers unimportant: Aunque sea mi hermano, no le dejo dinero (Even if he is my brother — and he is — I won’t lend him money).
2. Por mucho que / por más que
These structures insist on EFFORT or INTENSITY: however much you do something, the result doesn’t change. They’re usually used with the subjunctive:
However much I study, it won’t go into my head.
However hard I try, I can’t do it. (indicative: a real, repeated fact)
However much you cry, I’m not buying you that toy.
With the indicative = you describe a real, repeated fact (por más que lo intento). With the subjunctive = hypothetical or general (por más que lo intente). The subjunctive is more common.
For the intensity of a QUALITY: POR MUY + adjective + QUE + subjunctive (usually with ser / estar):
However tired she is, she always smiles.
However fast you drive, you won’t get there on time.
Don’t forget “muy”: “por difícil que sea” exists, but “por muy difícil que sea” is much more natural in speech.
4. A pesar de, aun así, y eso que
A pesar de la lluvia, salimos. / A pesar de estar cansado, vino.
A pesar de que vive lejos, viene.
Aprobó, y eso que no estudió nada.
“Y eso que” is very colloquial and very Spanish. It adds information that makes the result even more surprising: Está delgadísimo, y eso que come como un león.
Por muy cansada que está, sonríe.
Por muy cansada que esté, sonríe.
Por mucho cansada que esté, sonríe.
“Although it’s cold (I know), I’m going out.”
A certain fact, new information → indicative.
“He’s really thin, and that’s even though he eats a huge amount.”
Está delgadísimo, y eso que come muchísimo.
Está delgadísimo, por mucho que coma.
Está delgadísimo, a pesar de comer.
However hard I try, I can’t do it.
¿Por qué quiere Costel dejar el curso?
Por mucho que estudia, no consigue hablar bien
The list of words Costel and Ana prepared for the conversation with his grandson.
An eighteen-wheeler lorry has, as the name says, eighteen wheels. Although that seems a lot, there are lorries with more.
The cab is where the driver lives. However small it is, it has a bed, a fridge and sometimes a television.
The trailer is the back part, where the load goes. Costel has carried all sorts of things: furniture, fruit, new cars and even a grand piano.
Although he drives at night, he’s never afraid. What he likes most are sunrises on the road.
He has driven more than two million kilometres, and that’s even though he’s never yet been to Portugal.
Una cama, una nevera y a veces una televisión

For three weeks, Costel prepared the conversation like an exam. He wrote it in a little notebook he always kept in the cab of his lorry. He practised it out loud on the motorways of Hungary, Austria, Italy and France. However many mistakes he made, he started again.

He practised with everyone. With the waiters at motorway service stations, who looked at him curiously when he asked if they knew how many wheels a lorry had. With other Spanish drivers, who laughed at his accent but corrected him patiently. And with Ana, on video call, every Tuesday at eight.

“Don’t worry about mistakes,” Ana told him. “Even if you say ‘el camiona’ instead of ‘el camión’, your grandson will understand you. And if he doesn’t, he’ll laugh. And laughing together is already talking.”

At the beginning of October, Costel had a job in Valencia: he had to take a load of oranges from the port to Germany. He called his daughter and told her he’d drop by on Saturday. He didn’t say anything about the conversation he’d prepared. He wanted it to be a surprise.

On Saturday morning he parked the lorry on a quiet street in the Benimaclet neighbourhood. It was a huge red lorry, with eighteen wheels and the company name in white letters. The neighbours came out onto their balconies to look at it.

His daughter came down to open the door of the building. Behind her, hiding between her legs, was Álex, his grandson. He was six, with black hair like his mother’s and green eyes like his father’s. He looked shyly at his grandfather, as usual.
“Hola, abuelo,” he said in Spanish, very quietly.

Costel took a deep breath. This was the moment. He had prepared for weeks. But suddenly, as always, his mind went blank. All the words in the notebook vanished from his head. All that was left was the silence and his grandson’s shy gaze.
Then he did the only thing he could do. He bent down, pointed at the street and said, in his terrible accent:
“Álex. Do you want to see… my lorry?”
The boy looked up. He followed the direction of his grandfather’s finger. And then he saw it: the red eighteen-wheeler, parked on his street, gleaming in the October sun.
His mouth fell open. His eyes widened. He let go of his mother’s legs and ran out into the street.
“Is it yours? Is it really yours, Grandpa?” he shouted, jumping up and down. “It’s a Volvo! It’s a Volvo FH with eighteen wheels! I’ve got one just like it, but small!”
Costel didn’t understand everything the boy said, because he was talking very fast. But he understood “Volvo” and “eighteen wheels”. And suddenly all the words in the notebook came back at once.
“Yes. It’s a Volvo. It has eighteen wheels. The cab is my home when I travel. It has a bed, a fridge… and a little television. Do you want to get in?”
Álex looked at his mother. His mother, who hadn’t heard her father say so many words in a row in Spanish in ten years, had tears in her eyes. She nodded, unable to speak.

They spent the whole morning in the cab. Costel showed him the steering wheel, the tachograph, the bed behind the seats and the little fridge where he always kept a piece of cheese from his village. He let him blow the horn. The whole street came out onto their balconies.
Álex asked questions non-stop. How many countries have you been to? How many kilometres does the lorry do? Do you really sleep here? Have you ever seen a bear on the road?

Costel answered as best he could, with mistakes, with gestures, sometimes with a Romanian word when he didn’t know the Spanish one. And the boy, instead of getting bored, started repeating the Romanian words: “urs”, “drum”, “camion”.
“‘Camion’ is the same in Romanian?” he asked, surprised.
“Almost the same. Look: you say ‘camión’, I say ‘camion’. Only the accent is missing.”
Álex thought about it. “Then Romanian isn’t that weird after all,” he said at last.

At lunchtime, Costel’s daughter called them from the balcony. Álex didn’t want to come down. His grandfather had to promise that next time he was passing through Valencia, he’d take him for a spin round the port in the lorry.
At the table, Costel’s son-in-law, a big, friendly Valencian called Vicent, served him a huge paella and slapped him on the back.
“Costel, you speak very good Spanish. Since when?”
“For a year. I go to classes on Tuesdays. And that’s even though I drive twelve hours a day.”
Vicent whistled, impressed. His daughter took his hand under the table and squeezed it hard, like when she was little.
When it was time to leave, Álex walked him to the lorry. Before Costel climbed into the cab, the boy tugged at his sleeve.
“Grandpa, how do you say ‘te quiero’ in Romanian?”
It took Costel a moment to answer. He had a lump in his throat.
“Te iubesc, bunicule,” Álex repeated, with a terrible Spanish accent. And he ran off to his mother, dying of embarrassment.
That Tuesday, Costel came to class with a crate of Valencia oranges for all his classmates. Ana asked him how it had gone.
Costel smiled, took a small toy lorry out of his pocket, a red Volvo with eighteen wheels, and put it on the desk.
“My grandson gave it to me,” he said. “So I don’t forget him on the road. And I promised him that, however hard it is, next year I’ll speak Spanish to him without the notebook.”

Nobody said anything. Then Mrs Ecaterina began to clap softly. Mr Dan joined in. And within seconds, the whole class was applauding a fifty-eight-year-old lorry driver who had been on the point of giving up.

Ana looked at the little red lorry on the desk and thought that, of all the students she had ever had, Costel was the one who had learned the most. And that’s even though he still said “el camiona” now and then.
That evening, when she got home, Ana told Mihai the story while they were making dinner. Mihai listened in silence, chopping onions, and at the end he put the knife down.

“You know what the most beautiful part is?” he said. “Costel didn’t learn Spanish for the sake of the language. He learned it for a six-year-old he loves more than anything in the world. Whatever the grammar books say, that’s the best motivation there is.”

Ana thought about her own daughter, Rosa Elena, who already mixed Spanish and Romanian in the same sentence without realising it. She thought about Yuki, who in a few weeks was getting married in Kyoto and had learned Spanish without ever having been to Spain. She thought about Mrs Ecaterina, Mr Dan, Andrei.
They had all had a reason. None of them was the language itself. It was always a person: a grandson, a son, a love, a writer dead for many years.
“Even though I sometimes get sick of marking,” said Ana, “I think I have the best job in the world.”

Mihai smiled and picked up the knife again. “And that’s even though they still don’t pay you overtime,” he said. They both laughed, and from the next room, half asleep, Rosa Elena laughed too, without knowing why.

Text to read: The message from Costel’s daughter
After the visit, Costel’s daughter writes to Ana.
Dear Ana: we don’t know each other, but I have to thank you. Even if my father doesn’t tell you, you’ve changed his life.
For ten years, however hard I tried, my son and my father couldn’t talk. It hurt me terribly.
Now Álex talks about his grandfather all day. He’s asked me to teach him Romanian. Although he only knows five words, he says them with great pride.
However far apart we are, I now know my family is united. Thank you for not letting my father give up.
